notes.text: The London System always starts with d4.
notes.original: This is always the first move of the London System.

notes.text: Against the Old Benoni, plain London moves are not advised, so you play a different system.
notes.original: The Old Benoni Defence. Against this defence, simply playing the standard moves of the London System is not advised. So we will play a different system instead.

notes.text: The London is a solid setup that avoids theory; learn its ideas and themes rather than memorising lines.
notes.original:
The London, characterized by the moves d4, Bf4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, Nbd2, c3, O-O, and h3, is a solid, flexible system opening that is increasingly popular among club players and masters alike. The main draw of the London is that it lets the white player avoid opening theory and just get to a solid, playable position every time by playing this set-up. While this simple understanding of the opening suffices at lower levels and the opening can generally be played without serious preparation, black does have plenty of options that will result in a bad time for a "typical" London approach (see chapters 2, 5, and to a lesser extent 6 and 9). Even beyond this, though, an unprepared London player facing "normal" play from black can easily find themselves struggling to generate play. The London gets a reputation for being boring, but the truth is far from it. In the hands of the right player, the London can be extremely sharp.
The aim of this study is to serve as a reference tool for the London against everything that you're likely to see from black and to illustrate common motifs in the London. As such, it should be skimmed, not seriously studied (outside of maybe chapters 2 and 5, because these are critical lines). What's most important with the London is picking up on ideas and knowing how you can play specific positions, more so than knowing exactly how to play specific lines (which only would really become relevant well into master-level play). Then if you've played a game where black really stumped you, you can look in this study and figure out in depth the optimal way to play. My hope is that this study will be useful for beginners and high-level players alike. Players who are newer to the London should be trying to digest themes and not paying as much attention to specific lines, but more experienced players might want to pay more close attention to some of the complex theory in here.
In the creation of this study, I have used my own extensive experience in playing this opening as a 2000-2190 (USCF) over the past 5 years, combined with knowledge from the fantastic book from Holmes and Predo, "The Agile London System," which I highly recommend to any serious London player. I also made liberal use of the opening explorer to have a better feel on what's typical at master level, and I used the engine occasionally to fill in some gaps.

notes.text: Black can play Bf5 before or after Nf6; either way you answer with c4 immediately.
notes.original: Black can play Bf5 before or after Nf6, but the move order doesn't change your response to it--c4 immediately. Also note c6, which also intends for an early Bf5 (and can be thought of as a little brother to the more potent 2... c5, covered in chapter 4).

notes.text: Copying your moves is a trick, not a refutation of the London.
notes.original: We've all seen it - your opponent goes for the old "mirror their moves until they make a mistake" trick when they don't know your opening. No matter their reason, this is not a refutation of the London.

notes.text: This quieter ...d5 line is the little brother of the Nf6 c5 line, and it can catch you off guard.
notes.original: Before we get into the more potent Nf6 c5 line, it's worth discussing its little brother, which can catch you off guard if you aren't prepared.

notes.text: This is annoying for London players, but White can't answer c5 with d5 the way Black can.
notes.original: Annoying for London players. Others recommend Nf6 c5 as an anti-London but the advantage of d5 c5 is that d5 is not an available response for white against c5.

notes.text: Black's bishop pins the e2 pawn to your queen, so e3 and Nf3 can't be played.
notes.original: Another Stockfish level 3 novelty... Annoying as now e3 and Nf3 cannot be played.

notes.text: Your best answer is c4, hitting Black's center and ignoring the flank pawn push.
notes.original:
Black can also play the uncommon 2...h5!?, and the bishop is trapped if if 3.e3? is played (3...e5 4.dxe5 g5 5.Bg3 h4 6.Bxh4 or 4.Bxe5 f6).

This sneaky and uncommon sideline sets up a trap to win White's bishop.

At first glance, this move appears strange, developing a flank pawn instead of a piece or central pawn. However, 3.e3? lets Black win the bishop for three pawns after 3...e5! 4.Bxe5 (4.dxe5?! g5 5.Bxg5 Qxg5 6.Qxd5) 4...f6 5.Be2 fxe5 6.Bxh5+ Ke7 7.dxe5, and thus White will have to change their usual e3 move and choose one of two responses instead.

3.Nf3 develops the kingside knight and doesn't block the c1-h6 diagonal for the bishop unlike 3.e3. It is quite solid and questions Black's premature h5 pawn push.

3.c4 challenges Black's center and is White's best move, ignoring Black's flank attack and instead focusing on the most important region of the board: the center. This can lead to aggressive play from both sides.

notes.text: Your pawn backs up d4 and opens the way for your light bishop to reach d3.
Black usually plays c5 together with Bd6; the exact move order matters little.
notes.original: Typically black will play c5 with Bd6. Sometimes it's after Bd6 has already been played, but the timing is mostly unimportant.

notes.text: Sometimes Black never plays c5, and this line shows how to meet that.
notes.original: Sometimes black won't play c5 at all, which is what this line will look at.

notes.text: Against this typical setup, e5 is a fine square for your knight, and Bf5 ideas are gone.
notes.original: A typical setup for black with pawns on d5 and e6 and the knight on f6. I actually really like playing against this as the e5 square is now perfect for white's knight and the e6 pawn gets rid of any Bf5 ideas. The position can also be reached by a number of other move orders.

notes.text: Your pawn backs up d4, so you can retake with a pawn if Black captures there.
Your knight adds a guard to the d4 pawn and eyes the e5 square.
The knight takes its usual square and stops Black's annoying Ne4 idea.
notes.original: Putting the knight on its usual square. It's also useful to have this move to prevent opponents from playing the annoying anti-London Ne4, where after Nd2 they can play Nxd2 Qxd2 (this isn't necessarily bad but if you like having familiar positions out of the opening it's probably not for you).

notes.text: With Black pressing d4, retreat your bishop to g3, then aim for Ne5 and f4 to open the h-file.
notes.original: The key difference in this line against the other one is that now black has pressure on d4, rendering leaving the bishop on f4 bad. When black plays c5 and then Bd6, you play Bg3, with the idea of Ne5 and f4 if black doesn't take and open your h-file.

notes.text: Be7 prepares Nh5 to remove your London bishop, but here you can keep it on the board.
notes.original: There are a lot of move orders to get here, but that isn't particularly important. What is important, though, is that Be7 sets up for Nh5 to get rid of your London bishop. In this way it's like Bd6, but you can keep the bishop on the board here. As a result, Be7 is generally weaker than Bd6.

notes.text: Retreat to g3 and let Black exchange there, which would open the h-file for you.
notes.original: Carlsen avoids a bishop exchange on f4 or d6 and dares black to exchange on g3, which would open up the h-file. In general Bg3 should almost always be played as the reply to Bd6.

notes.text: Black avoids the trade, though many players happily double your pawns and ignore the open h-file.
notes.original: Caruana doesn't want to trade here. However many players will jump at the chance to give white doubled pawns, ignoring the access it gives white to the h-file.

notes.text: Black wants to break with e5, but your knight can jump to e5 against almost anything.
notes.original: Black would like to set up to break e5 from here, which would put him firmly in control if he succeeded. Fortunately for us, he has no good path to do so, since white can play Ne5 against basically anything.

notes.text: Bd3 is the usual move, but Bb5 is playable too.
notes.original: The usual move is Bd3, but Carlsen shows that Bb5 is playable too.

notes.text: Qe7 is Black's most sensible move here.
notes.original: The most sensible move.

notes.text: With the queen on c7, Black aims for the e5 break.
notes.original: The obvious choice--now e5 is inevitable and no Ne5 can blockade it!

notes.text: Black's efforts to control e5 are futile, so this move is pointless.
notes.original: Black's efforts at controlling the e5 square from here are futile, so why bother?

notes.text: Black's c4 looks scary but often weakens Black; you play for dynamics with the b3 and e4 breaks.
notes.original: Looks scary, but in reality c4 is often a weakening move. Since black is locking in the pawn chain, white will attempt to play for dynamics. This occurs primarily through the pawn breaks of b3 and/or e4.

notes.text: Black can kick your knight out with f6.
notes.original: Critical move. Now black has two paths: play for f6 to kick the knight out of the extremely important e5 square, or play Bxe5 to create a "weakness" on e5 and eliminate the strong knight.

notes.text: Or Black can take on e5 with the bishop, removing your strong knight and leaving a weakness.
notes.original: Critical move. Now black has two paths: play for f6 to kick the knight out of the extremely important e5 square, or play Bxe5 to create a "weakness" on e5 and eliminate the strong knight.

notes.text: Black prepares f6 to kick your knight, but there is a tactical problem with it.
notes.original: Playing for f6 seems very logical to me. If white plays the natural f4, f6 should be pretty good for black, with e5 looming. There's an issue, though.

notes.text: Trading knights starts the swaps that pull Black's pieces away from the h7 pawn your bishop eyes.
If Black spots the trap and plays Qxd7, your sacrifice only gets a draw.
notes.original: Black might be aware of the trap and play the somewhat sad Qxd7. Now the sac can only obtain a draw.

notes.text: Trading bishops pulls Black's queen to d6, where your d-pawn can lure it further away.
Your pawn hits Black's queen and drags it to c5, far from its king.
A Greek gift sacrifice, even though your knight can't reach g5 yet.
notes.original: Greek gift? What? But the knight can't come to g5!

notes.text: Your queen checks and settles beside Black's king, ready for your knight to join through e4.
Your knight hits the queen, gaining a tempo to play Ng5, and you are nearly winning.
notes.original: Turns out it can. The discovery on the queen gives white a tempo to play Ng5, and now he is nearly winning.

notes.text: Your knight covers h7, so your queen threatens mate there next move.
Your queen takes f7 with check, guarded by your knight, stripping the king's cover.
The check drives Black's king back to g8, and your queen can come in on h7 next.
The h-pawn move prepares to bring a rook to f3 via h3.
notes.original: With the idea of Rh3-f3

notes.text: Backed by your knight, the queen checks again and sends the king back to the corner.
Rd1 is also worth considering here.
notes.original: Is worthy of consideration as well

notes.text: Black's knight was hitting your queen, so it steps away with check.
Castling takes your king out of the centre and puts a rook on the d-file.
Backed by your knight, the queen's check starts chasing Black's king toward the centre.
Another check pushes the king to e7 and lines your queen up on the g7 pawn.
You win the g-pawn with check, and your queen now hits the knight on e5 too.
The pinned d5 pawn cannot take your knight, so the king must abandon its knight.
You take the knight the king had to abandon, getting your sacrificed piece back.
Your king steps up and uncovers your rook's attack on Black's queen.
You are clearly winning: your king is safe, your pieces are active and the h-pawn is a runner.
notes.original: Now that the dust has sort of settled, white's clearly winning. Black can't take the knight because of Rd6+ and his king is in immediate trouble, while white's is fine. White is also significantly more active, and the h-pawn is a runner. And this is if black plays optimally--it would have been very easy for him to get himself mated in that mess. This shows one of many positions where the Greek Gift comes into play in the London. One second, black thinks that he is facing the boring London, and then the next he's facing a brilliancy that renders him losing.

notes.text: You take the queen, and your knight now attacks the bishop on d7 and the b7 pawn.
Your knight wins the piece back, leaves you a pawn up and hits the rook on f8.
You are clearly better.
Your pawn takes on c5 and hits the bishop, so Black must spend time recapturing.
Your knight returns to f3 to watch e5 and d4 and clear the way for castling.
Your king gets safe first, so you can answer Black's e5 push by striking with your e-pawn.
Your pawn stops Black's e-pawn from forking bishop and knight, and challenges the d5 pawn.
Allowing e5 is justified: the e5 pawn is shaky and your pieces are active.
notes.original: Another case where allowing e5 is justified. The e5 pawn is shaky and your pieces are quite active.

notes.text: Here Nxc5 no longer wins back a piece on d7, unlike the other line.
notes.original: The difference is that now if Nxc5 white doesn't get his piece back on d7.

notes.text: White can only repeat moves here, so the game is drawn.
notes.original: White can only repeat, 1/2-1/2

notes.text: Recapturing with the pawn hits the knight on f6 and drives it away from Black's king.
Here Black no longer has the c4 and Qb6 resource after you play f4.
notes.original: In this line, black no longer has the resource c4 Qb6 after f4

notes.text: Your f-pawn backs up the e5 pawn, which both black knights are attacking.
Your knight adds a second defender to the e5 pawn, now attacked three times.
Your doubled isolated pawns are not weak: Black can't exploit them, and you aim for c4 or e4.
notes.original: Doubled isolated pawns? Not as weak as they seem. Black lacks a way to exploit them. Black's kingside remains vulnerable thanks to the e5 pawn and white will be looking to play c4 if he gets the chance and if not shooting for e4. Due to his lack of activity and more exploitable weaknesses, black is the one in trouble here.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the bishop, which can't retake on c5 without exposing Black's queen to your bishop.
Recapturing with the h-pawn opens the h-file for your rook, straight at the h7 pawn.
Black's e5 break isn't good enough: he may not win the pawn back, and his center and kingside are vulnerable.
notes.original: Unfortunately for black, the e5 break isn't good enough. If he isn't careful, he won't be able to regain the pawn (such as after d4? cxd4 followed by Rc1), and even if he does his center and kingside are both vulnerable.

notes.text: Your knight on e5 is key; unless Black takes it, f4 comes next and secures it.
notes.original: Of critical importance. Unless black plays Bxe5, f4 will come next, securing your hold on e5.

notes.text: Taking back with the pawn attacks Black's knight and drives it off the kingside.
Pushing f4 is tempting but loses a pawn; calmly playing Nf3 is best.
notes.original: f4 is tempting, but loses a pawn. Although there is perhaps compensation, it's best to play Nf3.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn may look weak, but that is a mirage; Black's only try to attack it fails.
notes.original: The e5 pawn may look weak, but it is a mirage. Black has only one way to try to exploit it and it's a total failure

notes.text: Black's f6 is his only sensible try: it breaks the bind of your e5 pawn and frees his center.
notes.original: In my eyes the only sensible way for black to play this position. He could also go for a6 and b5 and a queenside attack, but this seems weak compared to white's prospects on the kingside and in the center. f6 breaks the bind created by the e5 pawn, which in turn potentially activates his center and certainly allows him to defend his kingside.

notes.text: Black piles up on the e5 pawn, but is it really free?
notes.original: Free pawn?

notes.text: You trade off the e5 pawn before Black's three attackers win it.
Don't let Black get e5; with your knight there and his f-pawn gone, you are better.
notes.original: Don't let black get e5! In many situations, if black breaks e5 you've failed. With certain control of the e5 square, more activity, and some weaknesses created by the absence of the f6 pawn, white is better here.

notes.text: You castle and leave e5 as bait: taking it lets your queen attack Black's king.
If Black simply takes on e5, recapture, then play e4 and develop normally while watching the kingside.
notes.original: Black can also choose to not play stupidly from here, and if so you'll be looking to play e4 and developing normally while keeping an eye out for opportunities on the kingside.

notes.text: Take back: whatever recaptures on e5 lands in your bishop's line to Black's queen.
Your queen hits the pinned knight on e5 and joins the bishop against h7.
You are winning.
You usually play Ne5 here, but Black does fine in that line, so this messy e4 is the modern choice.
notes.original: Traditionally, I play Ne5 here. I've found that black is totally fine in that line, though, so I have to adapt to the times and go into this mess.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the knight and chases it away from guarding Black's king.
Sharp play like this shows the London is not drawish or boring.
notes.original: And people complain that the London is "drawish" and "boring!"

notes.text: A quieter option: a3 prepares b4 if Black allows it.
notes.original: Is also viable if you're boring like me. You want b4 if black allows it.

notes.text: You win the piece back and threaten mate on h7 with queen and bishop.
Your queen steps away from the pawn and guards the knight Black's bishop is attacking.
Follow with h5 for a strong attack; this line has done well at master level.
notes.original: Followed by h5 and a potent attack. I'm not going to go into further detail on this line because I've never played it in a real game--when I do see b6 (which is less often) I play Ne5. It appears that e4 followed by this mess is now preferred, but I'm not experienced enough in it to really evaluate this well. White has had good success at master level (and even just in the lichess database) with this line, at least. It's too complicated for me to get into here, especially without experience, though.

notes.text: Of course: Black plays a5 to stop your b4.
notes.original: Of course

notes.text: You still have kingside ambitions: the h5 knight is vulnerable to a discovery and h7 is shaky.
notes.original: Black has tons of options on how to play this position. As for you, you still have ambitions on the kingside, since the h5 knight is vulnerable to a discovery and h7 is questionable. For example:

notes.text: This time you keep the pawn; once Black plays a5, your whole game belongs on the kingside.
notes.original: Like the other line, but now you don't lose a pawn! Of course, this is just one of many ways black could play. No matter what, after a5 your entire game is on the kingside and you should be playing accordingly.

notes.text: Your knight takes back in the center, attacking Black's bishop on d6 and knight on f6.
Your bishop takes back and attacks the unguarded knight on c6, with the rook behind it.
Taking opens the d-file for your queen and makes Black's bishop leave d6 to recapture.
Your queen and bishop both hit the c6 knight, which has only one defender.
You are very active, and Black is one slip away from losing.
notes.original: White is very active and black is one slip away from a loss.

notes.text: Threats abound: b4 is extremely dangerous and Black has no counter.
notes.original: Threats abound. b4 presents extreme danger and black has no counter. For example:

notes.text: Your pawn chases the c5 bishop and is ready to push on at the knight.
Your pawn drives the knight off c6, where it shielded the b7 bishop from yours.
Your bishop attacks the queen, and your pieces cover most of its escape squares.
You are winning.
Your bishop gives itself up to drag the king out, so your queen can swing across with check.
Your queen checks the king, and your knight jumps to g5 next, aiming at h7.
The game ended 1-0 in White's favor.
Keep the bishop on f4 until Black plays c5; meanwhile you control the e5 square completely.
notes.original: Bg3 is the "normal" move here, but I prefer to leave the bishop on f4 until black plays c5 (which would transpose into the other lines after you immediately play Bg3). Without c5, the bishop is totally fine on f4 and black will be giving himself a headache by allowing your total control of the e5 square.

notes.text: Black can leave the bishops on the board, which leads to some interesting consequences.
notes.original: Black can choose to leave the bishops as they are, causing some interesting consequences

notes.text: You take the bishop back, and your new f4 pawn adds a second guard on e5.
This is what you will typically see below master level.
notes.original: What you'll typically see below master level.

notes.text: This is the best line for Black, but you rarely see it below master level.
notes.original: The best line, but also one that you rarely see below master level.

notes.text: Another good line for you that you're unlikely to meet.
notes.original: Yet another good line that you're unlikely to see.

notes.text: This stops Black's queen from becoming annoying on d6.
notes.original: Stopping Qd6 from being annoying

notes.text: Black should play c5 to transpose; Nbd7 is similar but a little worse for him.
notes.original: Black should play c5, and then it'd transpose to the 5... c5 line. He could also play Nbd7 here, which would play similarly to this but a little worse for him.

notes.text: Your knight on e5 is powerful and hard to remove, and taking it is a disaster for Black.
notes.original: You could play Bd3 first, but there isn't really any reason to not rush this out. On e5, the knight is very powerful. Positioned centrally inside of black's territory, it controls a ton of space and really limits black's ability to generate any play. What makes it a monster is that it's very hard to remove. Any attempt to take will leave black without defenders on the kingside, which can even be immediately game-losing sometimes. Trying to force it out with f6 can be dangerous on the kingside and, at the very least, makes e6 weak. To do anything, black must extricate the knight from e5. But doing so is a disaster for him.

notes.text: Black may take, since your e5 knight is powerful and annoying.
notes.original: Black might choose to take, since the e5 knight is powerful and quite annoying.

notes.text: Black may try f6 to kick out your knight, or reroute a knight to f5.
notes.original: Maybe he doesn't, though. Perhaps he thinks he can kick it out with f6, or perhaps he thinks that he can play the thematic Ne7-f5, perhaps even with Nd6 and dropping a knight on e4 to follow.

notes.text: You win the knight back, and your e5 pawn now chases Black's knight off f6.
You want Bd3, Nd2, f4 and Nf3, but Black threatens c5 and Qb6, so Nd2 comes first.
notes.original: In general, you want Bd3, Nd2, f4, and Nf3 here. However, move order matters. Black is threatening the always-annoying c5 and Qb6, so you have to play Nd2 first.

notes.text: Your knight comes out first, ready to reach f3 and hold d4 against Black's queenside play.
With no kingside defender, Qh5 is a real threat; if Black wastes time, he will be crushed.
notes.original: Due to the lack of a defender (because your pawn on e5 displaces it) you have immediate threats here with Qh5. If black wastes time in trying to deal with your hold on e5, he will be crushed.

notes.text: Black plays a calm, non-urgent move, but it lets you strike with Qh5.
notes.original: Just one normal, non-urgent move. What's the worst that could happen?

notes.text: Your queen joins the bishop against h7, so Black must loosen its king's pawns.
Black's pawn structure is a disaster, and Qh5-Qh3 exploits it.
notes.original: So many weaknesses, so little time. Black's pawn structure is a disaster, and this Qh5-Qh3 maneuver really exploits it

notes.text: Your f-pawn secures the prized e5 pawn.
notes.original: Important to secure your prized e5 pawn.

notes.text: Only you can win: better center, better pawns, and a potent kingside attack against passive Black pieces.
notes.original: Only white has any chance to win. Black's knight and bishop have nowhere to go, you permanently have the better center and pawn structure, and your attack on the kingside will be potent even if black plays f5. The only fear that you should have is black managing a fortress, but it'll be hard. This sort of position is what happens if black plays normally after Bxf4. If black doesn't immediately sue for activity, the strength of the knight on e5 will be overwhelming, and if he takes, the e5 pawn will create a defensive nightmare for black. This line shows off how sharply carelessness from black can be punished, and how leaving the bishop on f4 in positions without c5 being played is very viable, despite being less commonly seen.

notes.text: Your queen wins the pawn back with check and now hits the loose d5 pawn.
Your queen takes on d5 and gains a pawn.
notes.original: Gains a pawn

notes.text: This is the same attack explained in the line after Black's b6.
notes.original: See the line following 10... b6

notes.text: With no kingside defence, Qh5 forces Black to create weaknesses.
notes.original: It's thematic in these lines where black has no defense on the kingside to play Qh5 to force black to create weaknesses.

notes.text: Your g-pawn joins the queen and bishop against f5 to rip open Black's king.
Black could play Qe8, but you can just win a pawn by taking on f5.
notes.original: Or Qe8, but you can just win a pawn by taking and playing gxf5

notes.text: Your queen slips in beside Black's king and keeps its eye on the g6 pawn.
A rare queenside castle in the London: it lets you play Rdg1 and h4-h5.
notes.original: One of the rare times where you'd end up castling queenside in the London. You do so to be able to play, for example, Rdg1 and h4-h5. White is absolutely demolishing

notes.text: Your bishop gives itself up to strip the king's cover and threatens mate on h7.
Your queen takes the last pawn in front of Black's king, forcing it into the corner.
Your queen checks again and lines up on the unguarded e6 pawn.
There is no escape: your rook lines up on the g-file against the king.
notes.original: There's no escape

notes.text: Next come h4 and h5, which will crush Black.
notes.original: Followed by h4 and h5, crushing

notes.text: Nf3 means Qd2 answers Qb6, and if Black takes on d4 you recapture with the c-pawn.
notes.original: You want f4, but it's not totally necessary. You play Nf3 so that you can just play Qd2 against Qb6. Now it's not even a threat. If black takes, cxd4. Like in the other lines, you'll be much more active than black and have a very strong center and kingside attack.

notes.text: Your bishop points at h7 and guards e4 against Black's knight.
Your knight also covers e4 and can go to f3 to back up the e5 knight.
g4 is a thematic London attack when Black can't defend the kingside, and your e5 knight makes it work.
notes.original: g4 is thematic in the London when black is ill-suited to defend on the kingside, and this is one of those cases where it comes into play. Since black's LSB is unable to do anything over there, you have enough of an advantage to go for this direct attack. Take note that this is made potent by the knight on e5, which allows for this.

notes.text: The g-pawn hits the f6 knight; use activity like this to stop Black getting a strong knight on e4.
notes.original: It's important to prevent black playing Ne4 and attaining his own monster knight. If you carelessly played Ndf3 here, that's what you'd see. You don't always have to do it like this (something more simple like Qf3 will suffice in most lines) but when there's opportunity to prevent it with activity, go for it.

notes.text: Your second knight backs up the one on e5, ready to replace it if Black trades.
Your pawns bear down on Black, who must somehow deal with your knight on e5.
notes.original: With your pawns bearing down, black's in big trouble. Normal moves won't suffice; black has to deal with your e5 knight.

notes.text: Your knight steps away from the f6 pawn and joins your g-pawn in attacking it.
Black lacks play and e6 is weak, while your king is safe in the center.
notes.original: Once again, black just lacks play. e6 is weak. One false move and his kingside crumbles, while your king is safe in the center. His entire position is shaky, as your control of e5 has limited his activity and then forced him to create weaknesses to deal with it. White is much better, if not winning.

notes.text: You win the knight back, and the e5 pawn keeps Black's knight out of f6.
Your queen guards the f4 pawn that Black's queen is attacking.
This is the most natural way Black plays this position.
notes.original: The most natural way black would play this position

notes.text: Your knight covers e4 and clears the back rank so you can castle long.
Your bishop takes aim at the h7 pawn in front of Black's castled king.
A solid, standard London; your c3 knight is a bit misplaced but threatens Nb5, and kingside chances remain.
notes.original: With a perfectly solid, relatively standard London position. The knight being on c3 is perhaps not entirely ideal, but it does at least threaten Nb5. Even with it being a little misplaced, prospects on the kingside remain.

notes.text: Your pawn backs up d4 now that Black's c-pawn is attacking it.
Qb6 is annoying, so centralize your queen and take away its power.
notes.original: Qb6 is annoying. Might as well centralize the queen and stop it from being powerful.

notes.text: Your bishop comes out toward Black's kingside and clears the way to castle.
Your d3 bishop is strong and you keep a firm hold on e5.
notes.original: Your d3 bishop is strong and you have a firm hold on e5. White's solidly better.

notes.text: This line is boring; in c5 lines you want to avoid recapturing on d4 with a pawn.
notes.original: This line is boring. The main thing you want to avoid in these c5 lines is having to recapture with the pawn. It's basically always bad for you.

notes.text: Take back with the knight, not a pawn, so a piece sits in the centre.
Develop the bishop to d3, castle, and keep your knights where they are to control e5.
notes.original: The basic idea. Again, you don't want cxd4. If black takes, then Qxd4. If not, you can play Bd3 (after this, recapture with the knight if Nxd4), castle, and enjoy a rock solid, slightly better position. I'd spend more time on this middlegame, but you're not likely to see it, so you really only need to know the basics. Just control e5 as best as you can and leave your knights where they are.

notes.text: It's annoying for Black to regain the pawn, but don't trade off your d-pawn carelessly.
notes.original: Good for the same reason that the other line is good. It's annoying for black to regain that pawn and you're decently active. Don't be trading off your d-pawn willy-nilly though, it's important.

notes.text: Play this quickly so a knight on f3 can support the coming Ne5.
notes.original: Best to play this quickly so that you can support the inevitable Ne5 with N(d)f3

notes.text: Your bishop takes its best diagonal, guarding e4 and pointing at Black's king.
Your pawn props up d4 so you hold the centre instead of taking on c5.
Following up with c4 is also fine, but keeping it standard is simpler.
notes.original: followed by c4 is viable as well, but it's simpler to keep it standard for now.

notes.text: Skipping Bg3 earns a tempo; you can still play Bg3 and f4 to reach the typical line.
notes.original: This shows the advantage of not stopping to play Bg3 after Bd6 if black hasn't played c5 yet. You effectively have an extra tempo, and if you want you can use it to play Bg3 and then f4 as well, transposing into the more typical line. Depending on how things go, not playing Bg3 if black delays c5 is either irrelevant or helps you.

notes.text: Your pawn recaptures and hits the f6 knight, driving it away from Black's king.
Black may be tempted to play Qc7 and try to pick up the e5 pawn.
notes.original: In this position, black may be tempted to play Qc7 and try to pick up the pawn.

notes.text: Black challenges e5 to get a knight back to f6; expect to see this often.
notes.original: Sensible move to get a knight back on f6, expect to see it in positions like this

notes.text: The Greek gift works because your e5 pawn keeps a knight off f6, leaving Black's king defenseless.
notes.original: The greek gift sacrifice is a very important thing to keep in mind in these Ne5 lines. The e5 pawn displaces the knight from f6, leaving black defenseless (are you seeing the power of controlling e5 yet?)

notes.text: Your knight checks the king and clears the queen's diagonal toward h5.
Your queen checks down the diagonal the bishop left; Black's only block is the f-pawn.
Taking en passant uncovers your queen's check and opens your bishop onto Black's queen.
Black had to play f5, but that opens your bishop's diagonal onto his queen.
notes.original: Black had no choice but to play f5, but that opens up your bishop to win his queen. Strong activity lurks beneath the surface of the "boring" London

notes.text: Trading pawns keeps the e5 square under your bishop's and knight's control.
This Ne5 setup should feel familiar from the earlier lines.
notes.original: This position sure feels familiar...

notes.text: If Black captures on d4, you simply recapture with the knight.
notes.original: And if black captures on d4, Nxd4

notes.text: Regaining the pawn on c5 can be a nuisance for Black and leaves you active.
notes.original: Regaining the pawn can be a nuisance for black and you have good activity

notes.text: Ne5 is the best way to preserve your f4 bishop, though other options exist.
notes.original: I like this move because it's the only good way to preserve the f4 bishop, but there are other options.

notes.text: Bd3 is the normal move here.
notes.original: Normal move

notes.text: h3 is a typical move, but the author doesn't like it in this position.
notes.original: A typical move, but I don't like it here because of

notes.text: Black is restricted and must deal with your e5 knight, either by Nxe5 or by Nd7.
notes.original: And now black's a little restricted. He can't go for the normal fianchetto of his LSB because of his knight on c6 (which normally would go to e7 and f5 but can't because black played Be7). Qb6 doesn't accomplish anything because of Rb1. Black has only two courses of action--deal with the knight on e5 with Nxe5, or deal with it by Nd7.

notes.text: Recapturing with the pawn hits the f6 knight and pushes it off the kingside.
The Pereyra Attack: delay castling and aim a knight at g5 for a sacrifice on h7.
notes.original: This move characterizes the Pereyra Attack, wherein white delays castling and goes for a quick Ne5, h4, and looks for Nf3-g5 and a sac on h7. Playing Ne5 allows you the flexibility to go for this, but you could also play the typical Qh5, which is very good in this position.

notes.text: Black's f5 pawn tries to close the diagonal from your bishop to h7.
notes.original: Black has to do something about white's threats. One option is to try to close the b1-h7 diagonal.

notes.text: Hitting f5 with g4 is obvious and strong, but the lines get complicated.
notes.original: Obvious and potent, but complicated.

notes.text: Black's queen hits your e5 pawn to test your idea.
notes.original: The move to test white's idea

notes.text: Defending passively with g6 will end poorly for Black.
notes.original: Trying to defend passively will end poorly

notes.text: Play Nf3 here, not the immediate capture on f5.
notes.original: But not

notes.text: You take on f5; the reason for it comes with the next move.
notes.original: Because of

notes.text: Your knight on g5 is very strong, hitting the h7 and e6 pawns.
notes.original: That is one strong knight!

notes.text: Recapturing opens the h-file, so your rook joins the bishop against h7.
Your queen takes back on g4 and now attacks the e6 pawn.
You remove the knight that was forking your queen and your bishop.
Black has won a pawn, but at what cost?
notes.original: Black has gained a pawn... but at what cost?

notes.text: Your rook on h6 prepares to triple on the h-file and support a sacrifice on g6.
notes.original: Simple but effective, looking to triple up on the h-file and supporting a sac on g6.

notes.text: Your queen lines up behind the rook, doubling on the h-file against h7.
Castling tucks your king away and frees this rook to swing over to the h-file.
Black had to play e5; otherwise Rh1 and Bxg6 would win on the spot.
notes.original: Otherwise Rh1 and Bxg6 win on the spot.

notes.text: You call Black's bluff: he can't block the bishop with e4 or Bf5, so he is helpless.
notes.original: Calling black's bluff. He can't block off the bishop with either e4 or Bf5. Now black is helpless.

notes.text: Your bishop gives itself up on g6 to rip open the h-file for your rooks.
Your second rook joins in, so all three heavy pieces line up on the open h-file.
The check drives Black's king into the centre, since taking your rook costs the queen.
Your f5 pawn now presses on g6, and Black is helpless.
notes.original: And now

notes.text: The Pereyra Attack shows how dangerous the London can be; this Be7 line is easier for you than Bd6.
notes.original: This line (the Pereyra Attack) shows off how dangerous the London can really be. However, if black plays more conservatively (such as with Nd7) Be7 is a perfectly sound line for black, which will result in a middlegame typical of the London that is solid and playable for both sides, with a slight advantage to white. Overall, Be7 is easier for white to play and can be very dangerous for black, so expect to see it less than Bd6. In this chapter, unlike the ...Bd6 one, I chose to exclude lines where black doesn't play c5 quickly because they either transpose or are irrelevant.

notes.text: Your pawn steps aside to uncover a queen check while it hits the rook on f7.
You are winning.
Your pawn, backed by the g5 pawn, attacks Black's queen.
You are winning.
Your rook pins Black's queen to its king along the seventh rank.
You are clearly better.
You trade off the bishop that tried to block, and your rook swings to h1 next.
Your second rook triples up on the h-file against the h7 pawn.
Your pawn strikes at g6, the pawn holding Black's king shelter together.
Your pawn hits the rook and the h7 pawn at once, breaking open the king's cover.
You are winning.
If Black takes your bishop, the d-file opens and your rook checks on d8.
This check forces Black to block on f8, where you trade and loosen the guard of h7.
If the queen takes back, it leaves g7 and your rook can take on h7.
Your rook takes the king's last cover, and your queen behind it keeps it safe.
You are winning.
The position is equal.
You open the g-file toward Black's king, and a recapture with the e-pawn loosens d5.
Your queen hits the undefended d5 pawn and clears the way to castle long.
Black has no counterplay, and you can find play both in the center and on the kingside.
notes.original: Black has no counterplay and white will be able to find effective play both in the center and on the kingside. Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: You threaten a knight to g5 and h5, and a sacrifice on g6; this looks dangerous for Black.
notes.original: White is threatening Nf3-g5, h4-h5, and potentially a sac on g6 if black plays f6. This position looks very dangerous for black.

notes.text: As in other setups with your queen on h5, this pawn thrust is a strong attacking try.
notes.original: This is similar to the line with Qh5 in chapter 3, and similarly strong.

notes.text: Your second knight backs up the one on e5, ready to replace it after a trade.
You take back with the knight to keep a piece on e5, backed by pawn and bishop.
Your bishop on e5 is firmly held by the d4 pawn, and you keep kingside prospects.
notes.original: White has the better bishop pair, firmly controls e5, and still retains some prospects on the kingside without the knights on the board.

notes.text: Black's c4 gives you the b3 and e4 pawn breaks.
notes.original: As we saw in the last chapter, c4 allows the b3 and e4 pawn breaks.

notes.text: This is an ideal London position, especially if you want to attack the kingside.
notes.original: An ideal position for London players, especially those who wish to attack on the kingside.

notes.text: You will lose your prized bishop, but the d4 pawn keeps your hold on e5.
notes.original: You'll lose your prized bishop but still retain solid activity and a hold on e5.

notes.text: Now your hold on e5 is questionable, and you can't gain the b1-h7 diagonal.
notes.original: Now your hold on e5 is a little questionable and you can't gain the very important b1-h7 diagonal.

notes.text: e3 is the only good move here; the alternatives are worse.
notes.original: Important to note that this is the only good move here. Observe the alternatives:

notes.text: Nf3 here puts you on the back foot; that's why Bf4 comes first.
notes.original: This unassuming move actually puts white on the back foot, as black can end up in the same very good position we'll be examining for white, but just a tempo down (which doesn't matter that much). This line is why Bf4 comes before Nf3. Without having to waste a tempo on Nf3, the following line offers no danger.

notes.text: Nd2 avoids the bad line that comes after Nf3, but the author finds it very questionable.
notes.original: It protects against the bad line that occurs after Nf3 (since the rook can move if the exact same moves are played), but it seems very questionable to me. The main reason for this is that after

notes.text: This is the latest Black can play Bf5: e6 would block the bishop in.
notes.original: And this is the latest that black can play Bf5, since e6 would block off the bishop and c5 Bf5 would fail:

notes.text: Black hits your d4 pawn; this move annoyed the author, but c4 is no real threat.
notes.original: A move that always annoyed me when I first started playing the London. I mainly feared c4 and cxd4. I show how to deal with cxd4 in the chapter "London System vs cxd4", and as the previous chapter showed c4 is not a real threat to the London System.

notes.text: For concrete reasons, c4 is the only good response.
notes.original: For very concrete reasons, this is the only good response.

notes.text: Your knight develops and adds to the c-pawn's pressure on Black's d5 pawn.
Black makes his own London bishop and wants to trade off yours.
notes.original: Black continues his ambition--creating his own London bishop and then trying to get rid of yours!

notes.text: Black's bishop pins your knight on c3 and limits Qb3; strong but rare.
notes.original: Yet another ambitious bishop move, creating an annoying pin and limiting the effectiveness of Qb3. A very effective, but rare, line.

notes.text: Black's bishop has left b7 behind, so your queen hits that pawn straight away.
Qb6 is the only move you are likely to see, though the alternatives are worth a quick look.
notes.original: The only move that you're at all likely to see. In fact, I've never seen anybody play either of the two (relatively) viable alternatives OTB, and almost never online. This is despite this line being pretty popular below master level for whatever reason. Still, it's worth taking a super quick look at the alternatives.

notes.text: Qc8 is passive; take on d5, then develop with Be2, Rc1 and Nf3.
notes.original: The passive way to defend the pawn. Note that Qe7 would leave black unable to develop normally with Nbd7. In this line, like in the Qb6 line, black is passive, lacking any real winning chances. You should play cxd5 and then develop from here with Be2, Rc1, Nf3, and you can look for an attack on either side of the board.

notes.text: This is a technically viable but weakening way to defend b7, and almost nobody plays it.
notes.original: The engine way to defend b7. Not a fun move to play, and people don't. I've never seen anyone play this, but it is technically viable, despite being weakening.

notes.text: This is the author's favourite London line: after c5 the position is all White.
notes.original: Now, after that obnoxious amount of nonsense about other lines and proper move order and whatnot, we finally arrive at our destination. This is my single favorite line in the entirety of the London System. This is for a couple reasons. For one, black has no winning chances, as you'll see. The resulting position will be all white, and it'll be a question of if black can hold on (perhaps even create a fortress). I've never lost a game in this line OTB, and I've seen it a lot (the fact that I see it a lot is the other reason). I'm not even sure I've ever drawn. Many of my wins don't even last 20 moves. As you'll see, white is absolutely dominating.

notes.text: Black's queen trade is forced: it has no retreat that holds the b7 pawn.
notes.original: Forced. Black has nowhere to retreat to hold the b7 pawn.

notes.text: You threaten Bxb8 and Rxa7 unless Black moves the knight or plays a6.
notes.original: Note that you're threatening Bxb8 and Rxa7 if black doesn't move his knight or play a6 (but there's no reason for him to play a6 now instead of developing)

notes.text: Your pawn backs up c5 and gets ready to push on to b5.
h3 gives your bishop the h2 square against Nh5; follow with b4 and Nf3.
notes.original: Not the "best" line, but an easier alternative because it avoids the complications after Nh5. Your London bishop is very important in this position. As such, it makes sense to immediately give it the h2 square against Nh5. In this line, you'll play similarly, with b4 following as well as Nf3, but you're unlikely to be able to get b5 off cleanly, as black will castle and play a6. Then you'll want Nd2-b3-a5, as will be discussed later. You also might go for g4 soon.

notes.text: This leads to complications, but they are good ones for you.
notes.original: Complications results from this, but they're good complications.

notes.text: If Black plays Nh5, you answer with h3 instead of Be2, and it still works.
notes.original: If Nh5, you play the exact same thing as in the other line (Bc7 to e5 after being attacked), except instead of Be2 to exploit black's vulnerable pieces, you play h3. It still works.

notes.text: An interesting option: follow with g4, b5, a knight trip to a5, and h4.
notes.original: An interesting option for white. This is followed by g4 and the ideas of b5, Nge2-c1-b3-a5, and h4. I think that Nf3 is easier and simpler, but this is great too.

notes.text: With a slower move order Black can castle and play a6 to stop b5; here you can still play it.
notes.original: I include this line because it gives me a chance to showcase the other winning idea (the main winning idea is just b5), which is relevant if you play a slower move order (like h3, or even just not playing b4 as quickly). In these cases, black will be able to castle and then play a6, stopping b5. Note that here it doesn't stop b5 and you can just play it, transposing into the O-O line.

notes.text: Black is in a pinch: if he ignores b5, bxc6 and Ba6 win a pawn.
notes.original: Already black is in a pinch. If he doesn't do anything, white can play bxc6 bxc6 Ba6, followed by Bb7, winning the pawn and the game. But if he takes his queenside is blown open.

notes.text: Your bishop ties down Black's pieces, and c6 next would win at least a pawn.
notes.original: An annoying move. This immobilizes his f6 knight, which otherwise would've been his only useful piece after Ne4. It also immediately threatens c6, which would win at least a pawn if black just played a "normal" move like h6. Black can play a6 to kick it out, but not without a cost.

notes.text: Black's rook stops your c6 idea.
notes.original: Preventing c6.

notes.text: You threaten to trade bishops on d7 and then take on e7.
notes.original: Threatening Bxd7 Nxd7 Bxe7

notes.text: Your knight goes after Black's only active piece, the bishop on f5.
notes.original: To get rid of black's only active piece.

notes.text: Black may be tempted by h6, but it loses.
notes.original: Black might be tempted to play this, but it loses

notes.text: If Black retreats the bishop to e4, f3 chases it, and it ends up trapped on b3.
notes.original: If Be4 f3, and if Bc2 Kd2 Bb3 Ra3

notes.text: You take Black's light bishop with check and keep both of your own bishops.
Black has no play and his pieces stay tangled; remember the plans rather than the minutiae.
notes.original: Black has absolutely nothing. He still can't untangle his pieces, and white can calmly castle (or put his king on e2) and start pushing his b pawn to devastating effect. He could also do the same with his h pawn. The best part is that black has no play whatsoever. This position is winning. The common thread with all these positions we've looked at in this line is that black has very, very little to do. His rooks are forever trapped in passivity, and his minor pieces will forever be worse than their white counterparts. White has black in a stranglehold and can exploit black's lack of play and general entanglement on either the kingside or the queenside. Overall, this line is a disaster for black. Despite this, it's one of the more common lines to see all the way up to close to expert level. After all, if you don't know how to play against Bf5, black is very likely to equalize. If you know to play c4 and force the queen exchange, though, it goes from a frustrating opening to play against to the most fun one to play against. For much of my time playing this line, my knowledge after the queen exchange has been a little fuzzy and unrefined, but I still have consistently destroyed people because I knew to go for b5, and if not that, Nf3-d2-b3-a5. Black isn't going to play optimally enough to test you, so you don't have to know the specifics of all this stuff well. Try to remember those plans and absorb some of the ideas underlying the tactics, as well as some of the secondary stuff like h3 being important and g4 being more or less free. Don't worry too much about the minutiae.

notes.text: Your bishop takes a knight and hits the rook, so Black has no time to take on g5.
This check drags Black's king to e7, where your knight's capture on f5 comes with check.
Taking with check pulls the e6 pawn away, leaving d5 for your other knight.
Your knight picks up the d5 pawn with check, so the trades end with you a pawn up.
You are winning.
Your bishop retreats to e2 so it threatens the vulnerable a6 pawn.
notes.original: Best to move the bishop this way to threaten the potentially vulnerable a6 pawn.

notes.text: Black's rook stops any idea of c6.
notes.original: Stopping any potential ideas of c6.

notes.text: Castle here; h3 would be the wrong move in this position.
notes.original: Note that h3 is wrong

notes.text: Black can trade off your London bishop, but most of the damage is already done.
notes.original: Black can get rid of your very powerful London bishop, but much of the damage is already done.

notes.text: Your London bishop gets a retreat on h2 if Black's knight or g-pawn chases it.
You trade off Black's knight rather than let it sit on its strong central square.
Double rooks on the a-file and push b5 to win at least a pawn.
notes.original: Followed by doubling up on the a-file and b5, which should win at least a pawn, and then the c6 pawn will be free to run. Black has nothing to counter this plan, so we can conclude this here.

notes.text: Your bishop steps away from the knight to a square guarded twice, leaving that knight on the rim.
Your bishop steps away from the f6 pawn; if the knight takes it, a pawn recaptures.
Next comes b4; you are still crushing.
notes.original: Followed by b4, etc. White is still crushing.

notes.text: Black's rook pins your bishop on a6 to the rook on a1.
notes.original: All of a sudden, black is in control. The bishop is pinned to the a1 rook.

notes.text: Black threatens Bd3, so your pawn must fall and your advantage goes with it.
notes.original: And black is threatening Bd3, so the pawn must fall, and with it, white's advantage.

notes.text: Your pawn takes on c6 and now hits both the b7 pawn and the undefended knight.
The bxc6 bxc6 Ba6 idea has won most of the author's games in this line.
notes.original: Most of the games I've won in this line have been because of bxc6 bxc6 Ba6.

notes.text: Pushing b5 is still the right idea here; this slower h3 is only shown for demonstration.
notes.original: Again, b5 is right here, but this is for demonstration purposes.

notes.text: Your knight heads for a5 through d2 and b3, a dangerous maneuver.
notes.original: Signaling a dangerous maneuver: Nf3-d2-b3-a5.

notes.text: Black has only two answers to Na5: b6 drops the a6 pawn, and b5 leaves a6 hopelessly weak.
notes.original: Black has only two options against Na5 here, since b6 would drop a6 and b5 would weaken the a6 pawn beyond the point of saving.

notes.text: Defending a6 with a rook on a7 looks unappealing, yet answering Na5 with b6 may also seem scary.
notes.original: Who would want to put their rook on a7 to defend the pawn? Probably no one, but playing b6 against Na5 might seem scary to some as well.

notes.text: Black leaves himself defending a6 in the most passive way once you play Na5.
notes.original: Leaving himself to defend the pawn in the most passive way imaginable.

notes.text: Be patient: Black can't play b6 unless you play Na5, and otherwise he has no play.
notes.original: Patience. Black can't play b6 unless you play Na5, and without that he's lacking any play.

notes.text: Black's knight checks you, but this actually loses a pawn; his other options were no better.
notes.original: What else could black even possibly do? It's very hard to come up with anything else, but this actually loses a pawn. If black doesn't play this, he'll have to maybe push g5 and then shuffle his pieces around, waiting for you to kill him. Might as well just go for this.

notes.text: You take the checking knight, trading off Black's most active piece.
Your pawn hits Black's bishop on e4 and forces it to retreat.
Your knight bears down on the b7 pawn, which nothing defends.
Your bishop grabs the pawn Black pushed; if the knight takes, your d-pawn recaptures.
You take back the knight and keep the extra pawn, with your knight still hitting b7.
You are a pawn up; Black is passive, and winning will be a comfortable slog.
notes.original: White's now up a pawn. Black once again is pretty passive, but the process of winning will remain a bit of slog. A comfortable slog, though.

notes.text: Sacrificing the knight on b7 is a thematic idea in this line.
notes.original: A thematic sac in this line.

notes.text: Your bishop takes a second pawn and attacks the undefended rook, with the other rook behind it.
Your bishop takes the rook; after the recapture your rook invades down the open a-file.
Your rook checks along the back rank and forces a Black piece back to block.
The c6 pawn will fall to Rc8, and your connected passed pawns will be unstoppable.
notes.original: The c6 pawn will fall to Rc8, and the connected passers will be unstoppable.

notes.text: Your knight wins the c6 pawn, and if the rook takes back your bishop skewers it from b5.
Your bishop hits the rook with the knight behind it, and the a6 pawn is pinned.
This shows the strength of your bishop pair.
notes.original: A demonstration of the strength of white's bishop pair.

notes.text: Black's b6 hits your knight on a5, intending a5 if you back off.
notes.original: The idea, then a5 if white backs off.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the unguarded b7 pawn, forcing Black's rook into a passive spot.
Forced, and Black's rook on a7 is locked out; you should create play on the kingside.
notes.original: Forced. This position looks unbelievably bleak for black, but it isn't lost yet. I've ended up in this position before and I was shocked at how resilient black's defenses actually can be (although I did win, so take that with a grain of salt). In fact, you should be trying to create play on the kingside, since the queenside is pretty solid for now and black's a7 rook is locked out of the game.

notes.text: Your pawn chases Black's bishop back and starts your kingside play.
Your h-pawn joins the g-pawn, preparing g5 to open lines at Black's king.
This lets you connect your rooks.
notes.original: You want to connect your rooks, and this gives you the chance to.

notes.text: You take back the knight, and the new c3 pawn props up b4 and d4.
Black wants e5, so keep your bishop from being blocked by it; Bb6 is also threatened.
notes.original: Since black wants e5, it's best to keep your bishop from being blocked by it. It also would threaten Bb6 if black didn't play e5, but he won't.

notes.text: Your king steps up to guard the c3 and e3 pawns before the centre opens.
Black hardly has a choice, since he must deal with Bb6; his bishop challenges yours.
notes.original: Black hardly has a choice, since he has to deal with Bb6.

notes.text: You trade off Black's last active defender while its a7 rook stays tied to b7.
Black's a7 rook is stuck, so you are effectively an exchange up with plenty of prospects.
notes.original: I'm not going to take any more of your time showing this long, drawn out line, so here's the rundown of what's important: Black's rook is stuck on a7 until he protects c6 and plays b6, which will create horrible weaknesses and almost definitely lose at least the a6 pawn (you can just take and drop the knight back). Because black's rook is stuck over there, you're effectively playing an exchange up. On top of this, black continues to have no play, while you have plenty of prospects. This should be winning, but you'd have to be a little careful, because it's not going to be super easy.

notes.text: Your bishop slips away from the h5 knight instead of letting it be traded.
Black wanted to remove your powerful bishop, but that is a fool's errand.
notes.original: Black just wanted to get rid of your powerful bishop, but right about now he's probably realizing that it's a fool's errand.

notes.text: Black's f-pawn hits your bishop, but it takes away the h5 knight's only escape square.
notes.original: Black still wants to get rid of the bishop, but this removes the knight's only escape square.

notes.text: This is probably Black's best try, but few players would back off now.
notes.original: Probably best, but who'd back off now?

notes.text: Your bishop dodges the f-pawn and offers a trade that plants your pawn on d6.
You threaten Rxa7 to win a pawn, and Be2 to win the h5 knight.
notes.original: And this is like 11... Nxe5, but slightly little less bad (not saying much). White is threatening both Rxa7, winning a pawn, and Be2, winning a piece.

notes.text: Black is a pawn down and his position is in shambles; you are winning.
notes.original: Black's down a pawn and his entire position is in shambles. White is winning.

notes.text: The a7 pawn hangs, and saving it with a6 lets Be2 win a piece.
notes.original: There are many problems for black now. One is that a7 is hanging. If he plays a6 to defend it, Be2 will win a piece. If he saves his knight/bishop with g5, a7 falls, and black loses anyway.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the trapped knight on h5 and threatens a fork.
notes.original: Attacking the trapped knight and threatening a fork.

notes.text: Your pawn forks the bishop on f5 and the knight on h5, so one must fall.
You are winning.

This is the London system, a general set of moves for White that can be played against a variety of moves by Black (it is Accelerated insofar as White has played Bf4 before Nf3). Thus, 2.Bf4 can be played against both 1.d4 d5 and 1.d4 Nf6. For an introduction to the Accelerated London system, see the move order 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.

Playing both ...g6 and ...b6 to play in a Double fianchetto-style.

White's plans in the London system are generally to to play e3, c3, Nd2, Bd3 in some order, and plant their kingside knight on e5 via Nf3.

3.e3 is the most common move order. This defends d4 and prepares to develop Bd3.Once Nf3 is played, e.g. 3.Nf3, the opening has converged with the regular, non-accelerated London. 3.Nc3, instead of playing c3, transposes to the Rapport-Jobava London.

Black's two main approaches involve 3...c5 or 3...e6.

The idea behind the 3...e6 line is to play 4...Bd6, getting ready to castle quickly and threatening to trade off White's London bishop. White can drop their bishop back to g2, inviting Black to trade but after hxg2 White gets the semi-open h-file in return. In the e6 lines, Black's light square bishop often has difficulty developing. This approach resembles a Semi-Slav defence with colours reversed.

The ...c5 line has the idea to to prioritise ...Bf5 and ...Qb6 before finishing developing the kingside and castling. Black seeks counterplay by pressuring b2, which White left undefended when they moved their bishop early on. (White does not want to take the offered c5 pawn of course: they'd rather play c3 and let Black trade into them, so that they can keep two pawns in the centre).

Having committed to d5 already, the King's Indian-style approach with 3...g6 is less common but still playable. Black continues 4...Bg7, and 5...O-O. White usually includes h3, so there is a retreat square for their bishop on h2, and Be2.

notes.original: The KID is quite good against the London. It's a very annoying opening to face because it invalidates most of the normal ideas within the London. If black wants, he can achieve e5 regardless of what you do. Also, by playing g6, he makes the b1-h7 diagonal so irrelevant that Bd3 is wrong. Meanwhile, after d6 your London bishop will be less relevant. As a result, it's very easy for an inexperienced player to misplay the London against the KID by playing "normal" moves and then find themselves worse. When playing against it, you should be aware that black has two different ways to play it that require two different responses: playing for c5, and playing for e5. Against c5 you play c3 and Nbd2, but against black preparing e5 you play c4 and Nc3. These lines will be explored in more depth, but this general concept is very important to remember.

notes.original: The standard idea, accomplishing the same hold on e4 as Bd3 in a more natural way. Also prepares Rc1 and b4.

notes.text: Against the Grunfeld your bishop matters more and you control e5, so don't fear it.
notes.original: For the London player, the Grunfeld can be viewed as a less effective version of the KID. The KID is so effective against the London because d6 cuts down the London bishop's scope and controls e5. With d5 instead of d6, the London bishop is much more relevant and white controls e5. These two factors make the Grunfeld an opening that a London player shouldn't be particularly afraid of. However, the white player does have a lot of choice in the middlegame and it can be very drawish. Still, I won't cover it in as much detail as previous openings for black.

notes.original: Exchanging pawns would also be very bad, since it would open the c-file to devastating effect.
