notes.text: Your c-pawn backs up d4, so you can retake with a pawn if Black captures.
Black will usually play this capture sooner or later; its exact timing and the move order matter little.
notes.original: Most of the time black will play this sooner or later and when exactly it happen, as well as the general move order, is not so important.

notes.text: This branch covers Black not taking on d4, but your plans stay mostly the same.
notes.original: This line will consider what happens if black doesn't play cxd4. White's ideas, though, are mostly the same.

notes.text: Whenever Black plays Ba6, you exchange bishops, play Qe2 with a tempo, then go for e4.
notes.original: Ba6 is generally worth mentioning because weaker players tend to play it a lot at some point. When exactly it happens doesn't matter much, because white has the same idea regardless: exchange, play Qe2 with a tempo, and then go for e4. The absence of the bishops changes little as far as white's plans go. If black plays it too early (such as if he plays it before he's played Bb7), white can punish him in the center with e4-e5 after Qe2.

notes.text: Recapturing with the c-pawn gives you play on the open c-file and chances for e4 and e5.
notes.original: Generally in the London exd4 is the right capture. Either recapture is viable in the QID, but cxd4 seems a little better here. It allows white play on the opened c-file and opens the possibility for e4 and e5.

notes.text: Your king gets safe before you start the fight for the open c-file.
Your a3 pawn takes the b4 square away from Black's knight.
notes.original: Preventing Nb5

notes.text: From d2 your knight can reach a strong outpost on c4 if Black plays typically.
notes.original: Or the more normal-seeming Nc3. On d2, though, the knight has access to a potentially strong outpost on c4 if black plays typically. Also, black can instead play cxd4 after you've already played Nbd2, so spending much time looking at Nc3 is probably not necessary.

notes.text: Black's d6 is the typical move here; d5 is also an option.
notes.original: The atypical d5 is also an option.

notes.text: Your queen backs the e4 push and connects your rooks.
e4 is thematic: you get more space and activity, with play in the center and on the queenside.
notes.original: With a solid advantage. White enjoys greater space and activity and can seek play on the queenside and in the center. e4 is thematic in these lines for white, who can seek play both on the queenside and in the center.

notes.text: Your rook takes the open c-file, facing Black's rook behind its knight.
If Black takes on e5, you recapture and get a potent kingside attack.
notes.original: With a strong position that should feel familiar to a London player. Bxe5 would be bad for black after dxe5 Nd7 Nf3, where white will have a potent kingside attack. It seems that the queenside fianchetto only makes the position a little better for white compared to the main line with Bd6.

notes.text: Your knight develops to d2, where it supports a later e4 push.
Your king leaves the centre before you open it with the e4 push.
Your queen lines up behind the e-pawn, ready to push it to e4 next.
Your pawns now stand side by side in the centre, and e5 may come next.
If Black avoids this, you stay comfortably better with moves like a4, Bh2 and improving your rooks.
notes.original: If black doesn't go for this white enjoys a comfortable advantage with normal moves like a4, Bh2, improving the rooks, etc. Black has little going on.

notes.text: Black has problems: taking on e5 lets your knight hit c4, and exchanging in the centre leaves d6 weak.
notes.original: Black has issues. dxe5 Nc4 threatens to win a pawn, and if black were to exchange pawns in the center, d6 would be left weak and white's rooks would be strong. Trying to defend the pawn isn't much better either.

notes.text: Trading pawns frees the c4 square for your bishop to aim at f7.
Keep in mind pressure on f7, since Black's rook no longer defends it.
notes.original: An idea to keep in mind, playing against the f7 pawn now that black's rook isn't defending it.

notes.text: Your a-pawn guards b5, so Black's b-pawn can't easily chase your bishop off c4.
Your knight heads for f5, an active post close to Black's king.
White is dominant here.
notes.original: White is dominant.

notes.text: You take back with the pawn, keeping your centre pawns side by side on d4 and e4.
Your knight on d4 is very strong, eyeing b5 and f5, and Black's d-pawn stays weak.
notes.original: The knight on d4 is very strong and further threatens to jump to b5 or f5, and once white's rooks are centralized they'll be powerful. Black's d-pawn will always be weak.

notes.text: Trade the bishops, then your queen goes to e2 and backs the e4 push.
Your queen attacks the unguarded knight on a6 and lines up behind the e4 push.
Your e-pawn takes the centre next to d4, safely backed by your queen.
You keep a solid edge and can break with either d5 or e5.
notes.original: With a solid advantage. White has e5 against d5 and otherwise can look to break with either d5 or e5.

notes.text: With your queen guarding it, the e-pawn joins d4 to claim the centre.
If Black plays d5, answer e5 with a kingside attack; otherwise you keep the better centre and activity.
notes.original: And if d5 then e5 with a kingside attack; otherwise white retains some advantage from having the better center, more activity, and potentially play on the dark squares.

notes.text: Your bishop gets out before e3 shuts it in and watches the e5 square.
Your pawn backs up d4 and opens the way for your light bishop.
Black has chosen the Leningrad Dutch setup.
notes.original: Black plays the Leningrad.

notes.text: Treat this move as leading into a Classical Dutch setup.
notes.original: Here we'll consider this move to lead into a Classical Dutch setup.

notes.text: This Leningrad order invites an attack with your h-pawn; skip it and play transposes to the usual setup.
notes.original: A Leningrad move order that presents interesting attacking possibilities for white with h4. If white chooses to not take this path, it will transpose into the d6 g6 move order.

notes.text: Your knight adds another guard on e5, the square Black's d6 pawn wants to support.
h3 gives your bishop the h2 retreat and also prepares g4.
notes.original: Standard in the London to allow the bishop to retreat to h2, but here it also prepares the possibility of g4.

notes.text: Exploit Black's f5 by making castling difficult; the bishop is also more active here.
notes.original: White can play less ambitiously with c4, Nc3, and Be2 instead, but it makes the most sense to take what black has given you with f5 and make it difficult for him to castle. Besides, the bishop is more active here.

notes.text: Your king gets safe now, freeing the rook to support a later central push.
g4 is the most popular master move, but it probably gains nothing; playing normally is better for you.
notes.original: Like 4.h4 against the other move order, this aggressive move is rarely seen in lower-level play but by far the most popular move in master-level play. Unlike h4, though, this probably offers no advantage and playing normally would be better for the non-adventurous Londoner.

notes.text: Your knight eyes e4, backing the pawn push you are aiming for.
Now you play for the e4 break.
notes.original: And now white plays for e4.

notes.text: Your bishop steps out of reach of Black's knight and pawns while still watching e5.
Your rook lines up behind the e-pawn to back its push to e4.
The bishop retreats to avoid a d5 fork once you play e4.
notes.original: To prevent the fork with d5 after e4.

notes.text: An important break: you now threaten e5, which forces Black to exchange.
notes.original: An important break. Now white is threatening e5, forcing black to exchange.

notes.text: You take the pawn back and your knight lands in the centre, challenging Black's knight.
Black has some activity, but the weaknesses from f5, on e6 and the dark squares, leave him worse.
notes.original: And while black does have some activity, his weaknesses created by f5 (e6, dark squares) render him worse.

notes.text: Black's knight is heading to b6, so your bishop steps out of the way.
notes.original: Nb6 is coming, so the bishop moves out of the way.

notes.text: The bishop supports your plan of pushing the h-pawn to h4 and h5.
notes.original: With the plan of h4-h5.

notes.text: Your bishop matters little here; the f6 knight controls key squares, so trading it is equal.
notes.original: The London bishop is not so important here, the f6 knight controls crucial squares and so this trade is equal.

notes.text: The position is double-edged: both sides have chances.
notes.original: With a double-edged position.

notes.text: Your rook takes the open g-file.
notes.original: Taking the open file.

notes.text: Black intends to castle queenside.
Your bishop threatens to take the e6 pawn, but Black has an answer.
notes.original: Threatening Bxe6, winning a pawn... or is it?

notes.text: This is Black's only move to equalize.
notes.original: The only move to equalize.

notes.text: Black prepares to castle queenside, but it may come at a cost.
notes.original: Preparing queenside castling, but at what cost?

notes.text: Your activity and Black's unsafe king make this winning for you.
notes.original: White will be up a pawn and have better activity while black will be extremely weak and have an unsafe king. White is winning.

notes.text: Black's many weaknesses give you a dominant advantage.
notes.original: Black's myriad weaknesses give white a dominant advantage.

notes.text: Black regains the pawn by force.
notes.original: Black will regain the pawn by force.

notes.text: The position is interesting but roughly equal.
notes.original: With an interesting but roughly equal position.

notes.text: Once again, accepting the pawn is wrong for Black.
notes.original: Once again accepting the pawn is wrong.

notes.text: You threaten to take on h7, followed by the queen capturing on g6 with check.
notes.original: With the immediate threat of taking on h7, followed by Qxg6+.

notes.text: Castling doesn't help Black: you take on h7 and then win the g6 pawn.
notes.original: Castling doesn't help.

notes.text: Black's king is stuck in the center and behind in development, so you have ample compensation.
notes.original: The only way to deal with the threat, but it doesn't change the underlying reality of the position. Black's king is stranded in the center, he's far behind in development and has much less activity, and white also has a better center and can quickly go for e4 and look for breaks in the center to expose black's king. There is more than enough compensation for the pawn.

notes.text: Next you bring a rook to the g-file for a decisive attack.
notes.original: Followed by Rdg1, with a decisive attack.

notes.text: Accepting the pawn is a bad idea for Black.
notes.original: Accepting the pawn is a bad idea.

notes.text: You are clearly better.
Black gets basically an inferior version of the Stonewall.
notes.original: With what is basically an inferior version of the Stonewall.

notes.text: Your knight comes out to its natural square and keeps a grip on e5.
This is the Classical Dutch with b6 and a bishop on b7.
notes.original: Classical Dutch with b6 Bb7.

notes.text: This branch is the Classical Dutch without the b6 and Bb7 setup.
notes.original: Here we'll look at the Classical Dutch without b6 Bb7.

notes.text: The Stonewall setup seems dubious at best against the London.
notes.original: The Stonewall seems dubious at best against the London.

notes.text: Your bishop clears the way to castle and backs up the knight Black's bishop will target.
The fianchettoed bishop is there to control the e4 square.
notes.original: The point of the addition of this fianchetto is to control e4.

notes.text: Your king gets safe first, then the c-pawn can advance for more central space.
Your c-pawn takes space, covers d5 and frees c3 for your knight.
If Black plays Ne4 here, the game transposes into the line where Black plays Ne4 a move earlier.
notes.original: Note that black's Ne4 would transpose into the 7... Ne4 line.

notes.text: Black's knight hits your bishop; it is a typical idea, but the exchange favors you.
notes.original: A typical idea, but the exchange that it forces benefits white.

notes.text: Your queen lines up on e6, the weak spot behind Black's d6 pawn.
notes.original: The idea against d6, exploiting the weakness of e6.

notes.text: Your pawn challenges the d6 pawn, the guard that keeps your knight out of e5.
You trade off the d6 pawn and open the c-file toward Black's c7 pawn.
You swap off Black's dark-squared bishop, leaving its dark squares harder to cover.
The semi-open c-file and Black's weak pawns give you a firm advantage.
notes.original: The semi-open c-file combined with black's weaknesses give white a firm advantage.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen that guards e6, the pawn your own queen attacks.
Your queen takes the e6 pawn with check and wins back your pawn.
You are clearly better.
Black has to retake with its d-pawn, because moving the b-pawn uncovers the bishop on b7.
Your rook takes the open d-file with Black's queen right in its sights.
Your knight heads for d6 or c7, squares your bishop on f4 already covers.
You are in control of the position.
notes.original: White is in control.

notes.text: Your knight steps aside so your bishop on e2 attacks Black's loose knight on h5.
Bringing your bishop to f3 is a strong idea here.
notes.original: Bf3 is a strong idea.

notes.text: Your bishop challenges the one on b7, so taking your knight costs Black the a8 rook.
Black avoided taking on f3, which loses material, but this leaves Black's pawns comically weak.
notes.original: Bxf3 would lose material to Qxf3, attacking the rook. This move, however, leaves black's pawns comically weak.

notes.text: Your knight steps away from the d6 pawn and now guards your f4 pawn.
Your rook takes the half-open file and hits the unguarded e6 pawn.
Your queen lines up toward e6, ready for the c-pawn to step forward and open the diagonal.
Your knight hits the loose bishop on d4, and taking the knight opens your bishop's line to b7.
Your c-pawn hits b6 and d6, beautifully exploiting Black's weak pawn structure.
notes.original: Beautifully exploiting the weakness of black's pawn structure.

notes.text: The pawn steps off the diagonal, so your queen joins the rook against e6.
Your knight guards the d4 pawn, which Black's bishop was attacking for free.
You are slightly better.
Your knight challenges Black's knight on e4 and clears f3 for your bishop.
Recapturing with the knight develops your last minor piece and keeps watch over e4.
Your bishop challenges Black's unguarded bishop on b7, the piece that watches e4.
Your queen takes over the long diagonal and hits the unguarded rook in the corner.
You keep a solid advantage.
notes.original: With a solid advantage to white.

notes.text: You trade off Black's strong knight before it can settle on e4.
Your last knight develops by hitting Black's bishop on e4, making it spend a move.
Your bishop takes over e4 and hits Black's unguarded bishop on b7.
Your queen recaptures and attacks the unguarded rook on a8 down the long diagonal.
You are clearly better.
Your bishop gets a retreat on h2 if Black's knight chases it from h5.
Your bishop develops to watch e4 and the f5 pawn, and clears the way to castle.
Your c-pawn takes space and control of d5 before your knight comes to c3.
Your knight joins the bishop in guarding e4 against Black's knight.
Your king gets safe before Black opens the centre with its e-pawn.
Black wants e5. It is best to allow it, though d5 can prevent it.
notes.original: e5 is the point of all this. It seems best to allow black e5, but it's possible to prevent it with d5 as well.

notes.text: Your bishop steps back so Black's coming e5 push doesn't gain time by hitting it.
Your pawn attacks d6 and is ready to break through, even if Black forks your pieces.
Bc4+ would save the knight but lose the c5 pawn; your intentions are far greater.
notes.original: Of course white can just play Bc4+ and then retreat the knight to avoid losing a piece, but then the pawn on c5 would fall. White's intentions are far greater.

notes.text: You ignore the fork and let your pawn run on toward c7 and Black's bishop.
Taking the knight is best, since taking on g2 would create some danger.
notes.original: The best piece to take, since fxg2 will create some danger.

notes.text: Your pawn now attacks the bishop on d8, so you get your piece back.
Leave the g2 pawn alone: it shelters your king, and Black must give the piece back.
notes.original: The pawn actually provides some shelter for the king, and should thus not be taken. Now the piece must return one way or another, leaving white with an advantage.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the knight on c6 and will take it unless Black reacts.
You are clearly better.
Your pawn takes the bishop, so you get back the piece you gave up.
You are effectively a pawn up with more activity, but king safety could be an issue.
notes.original: With an interesting position. White is effectively up a pawn and perhaps has greater activity, but king safety could be an issue. White's better, but converting this position would be complicated.

notes.text: You attack on the queenside as in the King's Indian, but Black's kingside attack is more potent here.
notes.original: With the same idea as in the line with e5-e4 in the KID (attacking on the queenside with the benefit of the opened diagonal for the London Bishop), although black's chances look better here with a more potent kingside attack than in the KID.

notes.text: Stopping e5 with d5 is less promising than allowing it.
notes.original: This is less promising than allowing e5.

notes.text: Your c-pawn strikes at d5, the heart of Black's Stonewall, and frees c3 for your knight.
Your knight adds pressure on d5 and guards e4, the square Black's knight wants.
Your bishop covers e4 and clears the way for you to castle.
Black's bishop eyes yours, but trading on f4 would open the e-file for you.
notes.original: Bxf4, opening the e-file for white and strengthening his hold on e5, would do black no favors.

notes.text: With your king safe, you are ready to push your c-pawn and b-pawn on the queenside.
Black plays Ne4 to stop c5 and b4, which would give you a strong queenside attack.
notes.original: Otherwise white can play c5 and b4, with a strong queenside attack.

notes.text: Your queen guards the knight on c3, preparing the b4 push.
notes.original: Defending the knight on c3 to prepare b4.

notes.text: This pawn push is the crucial idea of the whole line.
notes.original: The crucial idea.

notes.text: Retaking with the e-pawn clamps e5 and opens the e-file against Black's backward e6 pawn.
Your b-pawn backs up the c5 pawn and starts your queenside advance.
Black looks for counterplay on the kingside.
notes.original: Black seeks counterplay on the kingside.

notes.text: Take the pawn before it takes yours on f4; your knight guards the newcomer.
Trading off Black's active knight leaves it with a bishop stuck behind its own pawns.
Your knight defends d4 and may reroute to f4.
notes.original: Defending d4 and looking at repositioning to f4.

notes.text: Black has no kingside chances and e6 is weak; you play in the centre and on the queenside.
notes.original: And white is straightforwardly better. Black has no real chances on the kingside, e6 is weak, and white can find play in the center and on the queenside.

notes.text: Your bishop watches e4, the square Black's Stonewall knight wants, and clears the way to castle.
Your f4 bishop gets a retreat on h2 if Black's knight chases it.
Black fights for e4 just as you fight for e5, but you can do it more effectively.
notes.original: Black seeks to control e4 like white seeks to control e5, but white can do so much more effectively.

notes.text: Your king gets safe and the rook covers f2 against Black's knight on e4.
Your knight takes the e5 hole, backed by pawn and bishop, and frees your f-pawn.
Your pawn kicks the knight off e4, the square Black's whole setup leans on.
You are slightly better.
Your pawn hits the d6 knight, pushing it back and gaining queenside space.
You dominate: pressure on the queenside, more activity, and a firm hold on the center through e5.
notes.original: With a dominant position. White bears down on the queenside and also has much better activity and a firm hold over the center with control of e5.

notes.text: This aggressive h4 is almost universal in master play here, though rare at lower levels.
notes.original: This aggressive effort at exploiting black's f5-g6 is almost universal in master play against this move order, but is somewhat rare in lower-level play.

notes.text: Black shouldn't ignore your h-pawn threat; pushing h5 gives you strong play.
notes.original: It's not a great idea for black to ignore the theat

notes.text: Black's h6 prepares to answer your h-pawn advance with g5.
notes.original: With g5 against h5.

notes.text: Your h-pawn rams the g6 pawn to pry open the h-file for your rook.
You give up the rook for the knight so your queen can land on h5 with check.
Your queen checks the king, ending its castling, and also hits the loose f5 pawn.
Your queen takes a second pawn with check and keeps Black's king exposed.
No immediate knockout, but Black's unsafe king and lagging development give you ample compensation for the exchange.
notes.original: There is no immediate way to exploit the weakness of black's king, but there is still ample compensation for the exchange. Black's king has no way to achieve safety and he's lacking in development and activity (which also can't be easily solved).

notes.text: Your pawn hits the bishop on g7 and drives it back to its starting square.
Black's position is rather bleak here.
notes.original: Is rather bleak for black.

notes.text: Your queen eyes g3, which becomes a threat once Black plays Bg7; Rg8 would defend everything.
notes.original: Threatening Qg3 once black plays Bg7 (otherwise Rg8 defends everything)

notes.text: Your knight develops, clearing the way to castle long and backing an e4 push.
Your king tucks away on the queenside and the rook backs up the d4 pawn.
Black eventually has to play this; if Black keeps stalling, you can find play elsewhere, such as with e4.
notes.original: Eventually this pretty much has to happen. If black keeps stalling white can certainly find play elsewhere, such as with e4.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the g6 pawn, which nothing defends, so Black's king must step up.
The king walk looks silly but is forced; the early f5 and g6 weakened Black's kingside.
notes.original: This looks silly, but black has no choice. White has exploited the weakness created on the kingside by the early f5 and g6. Black actually has some tenacious defense from this position, but white is obviously better.

notes.text: Your bishop dodges the knight and pins the e-pawn to Black's queen.
Your bishop keeps the pin on the e-pawn; chasing it again loosens Black's kingside.
This resembles Nfd2 against an early Nh5 in the King's Indian, but works better.
notes.original: Like Nfd2 in the KID against an early Nh5, but better.

notes.text: Black can't play Ne4 because of Be5, and has weakened the kingside for no reason.
notes.original: Black can't play Ne4 because of Be5. Now he's weakened his kingside for no reason.

notes.text: Your knight adds control of e5, the square Black's setup wants to push a pawn to.
Black wants e5 as in the Old Indian, but c6 prepares Qc7, Nbd7 and e5, or Qb6.
notes.original: Black wants e5 in the Old Indian, but against the London it is not so simple. c6 gives black the chance to play Qc7 Nbd7 e5 or perhaps Qb6.

notes.text: Your bishop gets a retreat on h2 for when Black chases it with e5 or the knight.
Your pawn backs up d4 and lets your light bishop out before Black pushes e5.
Black could also play Qa5+, then e5 after c3, with the same effect.
notes.original: Or Qa5+ c3 e5, to the same effect.

notes.text: Bd3 would be wrong here because Black answers e5 and then e4.
notes.original: But of course not Bd3 because of e5-e4.

notes.text: Your bishop steps away from the pawn's attack but still eyes e5 down the diagonal.
Your king gets safe and your rook comes in before the centre opens up.
You have a clear advantage, and Black lacks play.
notes.original: With a clear advantage to white. Black lacks play.

notes.text: You leave b2 to Black's queen: if it takes, you push e4 and develop fast.
Your pawn takes the centre and frees your bishop while Black's queen is off pawn hunting.
Your bishop guards the e4 pawn, because your knight on d2 is pinned by Black's queen.
Castling breaks the pin on your d2 knight, so it is free to move again.
Your bishop dodges the e5 pawn and keeps hitting it from a safe square.
You threaten Nc4 and then Rb3, trapping the Black queen.
notes.original: With the threat of Nc4 Rb3, trapping the queen.

notes.text: Your rook takes the file your lost pawn opened and hits Black's queen.
Your bishop takes aim at the f7 pawn and clears the way to castle.
If instead Qb4+ Nfd2 and white is much better.
If Black checks with the queen on b4, block with Nfd2 and you are much better.
notes.original: If instead Qb4+ Nfd2 and white is much better.

notes.text: Your knight hits Black's queen and guards the b2 pawn it was eyeing.
Your bishop blocks the check and hits the queen; the c4 knight is bait.
Your pawn hits the knight and uncovers your bishop against Black's queen.
Your pawn takes b4 from the queen, so pushing the b-pawn next would trap it.
You are clearly better.
Your bishop comes out now, before your e-pawn steps up and shuts it in.
Your knight backs up the d4 pawn that Black's bishop now eyes, and watches e5.
Your pawn props up d4 against the g7 bishop and lets your other bishop out.
Black switches the King's Indian move order to get e5 quickly, without waiting to castle.
notes.original: Changing the move order of the KID to achieve a quick e5 without having to wait to castle and play Qe8. This thus seems to present an advantage for black over the main line KID.

notes.text: Your bishop needs to retreat to h2.
notes.original: The bishop needs to retreat to h2.

notes.text: From h2 your bishop is out of the pawn's reach and still presses on e5.
You want c4 and Nc3, as is typical against e5 in the King's Indian.
notes.original: Now white wants c4 and Nc3, as is typical against e5 in the KID.

notes.text: Your pawn grabs queenside space and leaves c3 free for your knight.
Ne4 would have equalised; after castling you keep some advantage.
notes.original: Instead Ne4 would achieve equality. Here white will have some advantage, as can be seen in the KID chapter.

notes.text: Your knight develops and covers e4, the square Black's knight wanted to jump into.
You are slightly better.
Taking on e5 clears your d-pawn away and opens the d-file for your queen.
Play Qd2 and castle long.
notes.original: With either Qd2 O-O-O or Bc4 O-O and e4.

notes.text: Or play Bc4, castle short, and push e4.
notes.original: With either Qd2 O-O-O or Bc4 O-O and e4.

notes.text: Taking on e5 clears your d-pawn away and opens the d-file for your queen.
You have the same ideas here as against the other knight move.
notes.original: With the same ideas as in the position following 6... Ne7.

notes.text: The pawn pyramid on c3, d4 and e3 is complete.
notes.original: The pawn pyramid is now complete. Now we want to develop our remaining pieces: The two knights and the light-squared bishop. The knights will go to d2 and f3 and the bishop will go to d3.

notes.text: Now develop the knights to d2 and f3 and the light bishop to d3.
notes.original: The pawn pyramid is now complete. Now we want to develop our remaining pieces: The two knights and the light-squared bishop. The knights will go to d2 and f3 and the bishop will go to d3.

notes.text: With Black's pawn on e6, Bf5 isn't coming, so developing the knight to f3 is fine.
notes.original: Since Bf5 won't happen here, Nf3 is perfectly fine.

notes.text: Nf3 is safe here because Black has played e6 and you have played e3.
notes.original: Again, Nf3 is okay here due to the presence of the e6 pawn. In general, if e6 and e3 have been played then Nf3 is safe.

notes.text: Never take on c5 yourself; if Black captures there, recapture with the e-pawn.
notes.original: This is a common move used to meet the London system. We never want to take on c5. If black decides to take, we will recapture using the e-pawn.

notes.text: Nf3 is fine here because of the e6 pawn, but elsewhere play Nd2 first.
notes.original: At this point it's actually okay to play Nf3 (due to the black pawn on e6) but in other opening positions you'll want to play this before Nf3 due to some tactical tricks involving Qb6 and Bf5.

notes.text: Your knight is now safe on f3; this is essentially a London against d5 and e6.
notes.original: Now Nf3 is safe. However, it can be further delayed if necessary. This is now essentially a d5 e6 London.

notes.text: Your doubled g-pawns aren't all bad, and your rook now eyes the open h-file.
notes.original: The doubled pawns aren't all bad (the pawn on g3 can be used to probe the kingside and initiate an attack occasionally) and now the h-file is opened for the rook.

notes.text: The h-file is half-open for your rook, giving you many attacking ideas, especially if Black castles.
notes.original: So many good attacking ideas for white, especially if black castles.

notes.text: Recapturing on d6 lets Black's queen develop there, ready to push e5.
notes.original: Swapping on d6 allows the queen to be developed to d6, threatening e5.

notes.text: Taking on f4 isn't terrible, but it breaks your usual London pawn structure.
notes.original: Swapping on f4 isn't the end of the world but it disrupts the typical London pawn structure and may lead to further issues if black takes on d4.

notes.text: If Black takes on d4, you recapture with the e-pawn.
notes.original: If black takes we recapture with the e-pawn.

notes.text: Black's c5 is a common, good counter to the London, seen in Carlsen against Caruana.
notes.original: This position comes from a game between Carlsen (white) and Caruana (black) - masters do actually play this stuff! c5 is a common (and good) way for black to counter the London System.

notes.text: Again you form the pawn pyramid with c3, d4 and e3.
notes.original: Again, forming the pawn pyramid.

notes.text: Your c3, d4 and e3 pawns form the pawn pyramid.
notes.original: Forming the pawn pyramid.

notes.text: Black develops and guards e5, but you can often trade knights there anyway.
notes.original: Developing the knight. This also defends the e5 square. However, this isn't necessarily a problem for white - often white will swap a pair of knights on the e5 square before rerouting the other knight to e5 square via Nd2, Nf3 and Ne5.

notes.text: Don't swap bishops on d6 or f4; retreat your bishop to g3 instead.
notes.original: Another common idea from black. White certainly doesn't want to swap the bishop on f4 (this would break the pawn pyramid) but swapping on d6 isn't great either. Instead white should generally play Bg3 in these kind of positions.

notes.text: Black takes, and again the h-file opens for your rook.
notes.original: Now Caruana takes. Again, this opens the h-file for white.

notes.text: Black's queen attacks your bishop on b5.
notes.original: Attacking the bishop.

notes.text: Black guards against Ng5 ideas and attacks along the h-file.
notes.original: Defending from any possible Ng5 incursions, as well as attacks along the h-file.

notes.text: Black spends a move chasing your bishop, which isn't a good idea.
notes.original: Spending a move to chase the bishop isn't a good idea.

notes.text: The open h-file looks scary, but Black can't easily bring heavy pieces over, and your g-pawn helps attack.
notes.original: Castling kingside. Although the open h-file may look worrying for white, black can't easily get their major pieces over to the kingside. Also the second g-pawn could prove useful for initiating a kingside attack.

notes.text: Black delays releasing the tension in the center.
notes.original: Black delays releasing the tension.

notes.text: Black releases the tension, which later lets you counterattack with b3 and e4.
notes.original: Caruana releases the tension. Later on, this will allow for white counterattacks via b3 and e4.

notes.text: You will play the e4 break later, and White is in a good position out of the opening.
notes.original: Later the e4 break will be played. White is in a good position out of the opening.

notes.text: Your rook hits the queen on c3, and Black's queen is trapped.
notes.original: The queen is now trapped.

notes.text: Your queen defends the b2 pawn.
notes.original: Defending the b2 pawn.

notes.text: Now everything is defended, and White has an edge.
notes.original: Now everything is defended. White has an edge here.

notes.text: Castle kingside; castling queenside is dangerous in these lines, however tempting the open h-file looks.
notes.original: One thing to keep in mind if you are playing for the pawn breaks is that castling queenside can be quite dangerous in these lines, no matter how tempting the open h-file looks! Castling kingside is generally the way to go.

notes.text: If Black takes on g3, your h-pawn recaptures and opens the h-file for your rook.
The h-file is open for you, and your light bishop can still develop outside the pawn chain.
notes.original: For the swapping of bishops, white has now opened the h-file. Also, white still has a light squared bishop outside of the pawn chain which can easily be developed to a number of good squares: d3, e2 or even b5, while black's light-squared bishop will only be able to access the a4-e8 diagonal.

notes.text: Your bishop gets outside the pawns before your e-pawn steps up and shuts it in.
Black's g5 is positionally unsound but unsettling; it aims for the h5 and g4 advances.
notes.original: Positionally unsound but very unsettling. I found this novelty when testing the London against Stockfish level 3. The main ideas are h5 and g4 advances (also h4 if the opponent allows it).

notes.text: Your bishop stays on the b1-h7 diagonal, threatening Black's kingside.
notes.original: Keeping the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, threatening the black kingside.

notes.text: A key London move: the knight is well placed on e5, and your queen gets the d1-h5 diagonal.
notes.original: One of the key moves of the London System. The knight is well-placed on e5, and the d1-h5 diagonal is opened up for the queen.

notes.text: Black takes the knight; leaving it on e5 would not be good for Black.
notes.original: Of course, it is not illegal for black to not take the knight but leaving the knight on e5 can't be seen as particularly good.

notes.text: Taking with the pawn chases the knight off f6, weakening Black's kingside, where your queen guards g4 and h5.
notes.original: Originally I would take with the bishop here, but taking with the pawn is better. It chases the knight away from f6, weakening the kingside (as the queen guards g4 and h5).

notes.text: The pawn storm begins; Black's bishop shouldn't take on h4, since that opens the h-file for your rook.
notes.original: Now the pawn storm begins. Taking the pawn with the bishop is a mistake as it opens up the h-file for the rook. Here we see the benefit of delaying castling kingside in the London System - if white were castled kingside, the rook would not be able to control the h-file.

notes.text: The d4 square is a hole for your second knight, so bring it there.
notes.original: There is now a hole on d4 for the second white knight.

notes.text: The queen move prepares queenside castling, so both rooks can then join the kingside attack.
notes.original: Preparing to castle queenside. Then both rooks can be used on the kingside to devastating effect.

notes.text: Black tries to close the h-file with h6, but it doesn't work.
notes.original: Attempting to close the h-file, but it doesn't work.

notes.text: Black wins a pawn, but your rook becomes active on the h-file.
notes.original: This doesn't lose anything immediately for black, but is still a mistake - white loses a pawn but activates the rook along the h-file.

notes.text: You trade your weakest bishop for Black's strongest piece, the knight.
notes.original: The knight is black's strongest piece, while the bishop is white's weakest piece, so white chooses to exchange them.

notes.text: Black is in deep trouble here.
notes.original: It's easy to see that black is in deep trouble here.

notes.text: The g5 pawn will soon fall, and Black can't stop your control of the g and h files.
notes.original: The g4 pawn will soon fall and black can't really do anything about white's domination of the g and h files.

notes.text: This retreat is also good for you.
notes.original: Also good for white.

notes.text: Retaking with the h-pawn is the usual continuation after Black's knight goes to h5.
notes.original: The usual continuation after Nh5.

notes.text: The h-pawn push begins your kingside attack.
notes.original: Beginning the attack!

notes.text: Black's knight threatens to swap itself for your bishop on f4.
notes.original: Threatening to swap on f4...

notes.text: You ignore the threat and sacrifice the bishop on h7, a common London theme.
notes.original: … but white ignores it completely! Sacrificing the bishop on h7 is a common theme in the London.

notes.text: Your knight checks; Kg8 and Kh8 lose at once, and taking the knight is just bad.
notes.original: Kg8 and Kh8 both lose immediately, while Bxg5 is just bad.

notes.text: This is a big mistake: Black's king gets checked and your attack goes on.
notes.original: A big mistake.

notes.text: You are now clearly winning.
notes.original: White is now clearly winning.

notes.text: After the bishop sacrifice on h7 and this retreat, White is simply winning.
notes.original: This is just winning for white.

notes.text: Nothing defended the bishop on f5, so your queen takes it for free.
Your queen comes back to guard the a1 rook and offers a queen trade.
Your knight develops with an attack on Black's queen, forcing it to move again.
Your queen steps out of the attack and adds a guard to the pinned d2 knight.
Your pawn attacks the knight on e4, which is piling onto your pinned d2 knight.
Black's knight guards d2, so your queen, not your king, must take back.
After all the trades, White is clearly winning.
notes.original: White is clearly winning.

notes.text: White has many positional problems in this position.
notes.original: White has many positional problems here.

notes.text: Black's knight now threatens to trade itself for your London bishop.
notes.original: Now threatening to swap the London bishop for a knight.

notes.text: This move, or b4, causes problems for London players.
notes.original: Either this or b4 causes problems for London players.

notes.text: The computer says you are ahead, but this is still dubious for London players.
notes.original: Computer says we're ahead, but this is still dubious for Londoners.

notes.text: The computer keeps changing its mind about this evaluation.
notes.original: The computer is changing its mind constantly about what the evaluation is.

notes.text: The bishop retreats to h2 as planned.
notes.original: Retreating the bishop to h2 as planned.

notes.text: This is the point of c4 and Nc3: both knights put pressure on e4.
notes.original: The point of c4 and Nc3. The knight will be useful on d2, and the two knights together put pressure on e4.

notes.text: Now your f3 knight has nowhere nice to go; with a knight on c3 it could retreat to d2.
notes.original: Now the f3 knight has nowhere nice to go. With the other knight on c3 it would be able to retreat to d2.

notes.text: Your last knight develops where it watches e4 and backs up a queen on b3.
If Black captures on b3, your a-pawn recaptures and opens the a-file for you.
notes.original: Capturing on b3 would open the a-file for white.

notes.text: Black's pawn hit your queen, so you trade queens and then aim for the b3 and e4 breaks.
This is the computer line: now prepare the b3 and e4 pawn breaks, as in a typical London.
notes.original: The computer line. Now we can prepare to use the b3 and e4 pawn breaks, as in a typical London.

notes.text: Aim for pawns on d5 and e4 with knights on c3 and f3, and avoid capturing with the central pawns.
notes.original: In this system, we will put strong pawns on d5 and e4 and our knights on c3 and f3. It is important to avoid capturing with these central pawns (unless black plays some very strange response) in order to preserve the central pawn chain.

notes.text: This lets Black take on d4, trading your central d-pawn for their c-pawn.
notes.original: This allows for the elimination of the central d-pawn in exchange for black's c-pawn.

notes.text: This is playable and gives typical London positions, but Black gets a small advantage.
notes.original: Playable and will lead to more typical London positions, but with a small advantage for black.

notes.text: Also playable, but if Black doesn't take on d4, your e3 pawn blocks your bishop from f4.
notes.original: Also playable, but if black decides not to capture on d4 the e3 pawn blocks in the c1 bishop and prevents it from moving to f4.

notes.text: The knight blocks the c-pawn, but keeps it flexible and prepares e4.
notes.original: This move looks strange at first as it blocks in the c-pawn. However, it keeps the c-pawn flexible (it can still possibly move to c3 to block the a1-h8 diagonal) and more importantly prepares e4.

notes.text: You build a strong pawn centre, and taking on d5 would be a mistake for Black.
notes.original: Establishing a strong pawn centre. Note that exd5 is a mistake for black here.

notes.text: Taking on d5 allows you to play e5, attacking the knight.
notes.original: This allows e5, attacking the knight.

notes.text: This move order reaches the main position you already know.
notes.original: A transposition into the main line given in this study.

notes.text: Your bishop clears the back rank so you can castle next move.
A good position for you: develop the bishop to f4 and bring a rook to the e-file.
notes.original: With a good position for white. Possible ideas include a queenside pawn advance (with a possible Bb5 or Bc4), developing the bishop to f4, and moving the rooks to the d and e files.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the knight, the only piece guarding Black's d5 pawn.
The knight move doesn't actually save the knight from your attack.
notes.original: This doesn't actually save the knight.

notes.text: You win the knight your pawn was attacking, even though Black's pawn now hits yours.
The check gains a move, so your attacked knight can jump to b5 next.
Your knight escapes the pawn and eyes c7, where a check would fork king, queen and rook.
Your knight heads for f4, where it will hit Black's queen.
Your knight attacks Black's queen and pushes it into a queen trade.
You take the queen back with your bishop, which develops it and clears the way to castle.
Your king gets safe and your rook can come to the open e-file next.
You win the pawn back and stop Black trading knights on c3.
notes.original: Capturing back the pawn and preventing an exchange with the e4 knight.

notes.text: Black tries to retreat the knight to g5.
notes.original: Attempting to retreat the knight to the g5 square.

notes.text: Your pawn takes g5 away from Black's knight, so it has no safe way back.
Your queen attacks the knight on e4 and finally wins it.
notes.original: Finally winning the knight.

notes.text: Your queen takes the knight, leaving you a piece up for two pawns.
Taking the knight pulls Black's queen off c7, so your knight can fork there.
Your knight forks the king and the a8 rook, so the rook falls next.
Your pawn backs up the one on d5 and lets your light bishop out.
Black can choose a fianchetto setup like this one.
notes.original: Black can choose a fianchetto setup as shown here.

notes.text: Your knight comes out, watches the e5 square and brings castling a step closer.
One main option: develop your bishop to e2.
notes.original: White can choose from two main options here: Developing the bishop to e2 or playing a4 in preparation for developing the bishop to b5.

notes.text: The other option: play a4 to prepare developing the bishop to b5.
notes.original: White can choose from two main options here: Developing the bishop to e2 or playing a4 in preparation for developing the bishop to b5.

notes.text: Your bishop gets off the back rank so you can castle next.
A simple developing setup.
A more aggressive setup: your bishop on b5 hits the bishop on d7 and knight on a6.
notes.original: A more aggressive setup, exploiting the tactical opportunities on the queenside.

notes.text: You can put your rooks on strong files, hold the centre, and your b5 pawn may trouble Black.
notes.original: White has opportunities to develop the rooks to strong files, has a significant presence in the centre and has a strong pawn on b5 which may cause black problems.

notes.text: You take back toward the centre, keeping a pawn on d4.
notes.original: (This chapter is still work in progress...)

notes.text: Bishop to d6 is typical in the London, but here it's a mistake.
notes.original: Typical move in the London but a mistake.

notes.text: Despite Black's attempts, you have reached a better-than-usual London position.
notes.original: Despite black's attempts, we have now reached a better-than-usual London position.

notes.text: Pushing d5 is the way to really punish Black; the pawn hits the knight.
notes.original: Ne5 is okay but d5 is the way to go to really punish black's play.

notes.text: The engine likes Black, but doubled isolated c-pawns and no development make this position easy to like for you.
notes.original: Computer evaluates this position as +1 for black, and it's easy to see why. Double isolated c-pawns and zero development versus decent development and a lack of weak pawns - I'll take that.

notes.text: Swapping bishops is the way to go here.
Now just continue the London setup as usual.
notes.original: And now we just continue the London setup as per usual.

notes.text: Carlsen–Giri went c6 here, but Nf6 is good too.
notes.original: In Carlsen - Giri, c6 was played instead here but Nf6 is good too.

notes.text: Even with different opening moves, you still have the b3 and e4 pawn breaks.
notes.original: Different opening moves, still allows for b3 and e4 pawn breaks!

notes.text: Now b3 is on the cards.
Both sides have chances, and this line will feel very strange to London players.
notes.original: Again, with chances for both sides. This line especially will feel very strange to London players.

notes.text: Both sides have chances in this position.
notes.original: With chances for both sides.

notes.text: You threaten a knight check on c7, and Black cannot protect against it.
notes.original: Now black cannot protect against Nc7+.

notes.text: Your bishop steps away from the g5 pawn but keeps its diagonal toward c7.
Nf6 would be a bit more solid, but this line isn't about solid positions.
notes.original: A slightly more solid move is Nf6 but there's no point playing this variation for solid positional benefits!

notes.text: Your h-pawn hits g5 and forces g4, leaving Black little chance of g and h file attacks.
notes.original: This move solves some of the positional problems in this line, as it forces g4 with little chance of g and h file attacks.

notes.text: The lazy e3 is a definite blunder here; don't play it.
notes.original: This lazy London move is a definite blunder.

notes.text: Developing the knight has the same problem here as e3 did.
notes.original: Same problem here.

notes.text: Black's pawn stops your knight reaching f3 and makes e5 hard to reach.
notes.original: This prevents the knight from going to f3. This also means that e5 will be hard to reach. While this may not theoretically be good for black any London player is definitely "out of book" at this point.

notes.text: With f3 covered by Black's pawn, this opens e2 for your knight and frees your bishop.
Here the alternative London setup is the way to go.
notes.original: The alternative London System is the way to go here.

notes.text: The benefit of Black's g4 pawn: your knight cannot be placed on f3.
notes.original: The benefit of g4: The knight cannot be placed on f3.

notes.text: Your second knight develops and joins the c-pawn in pressing Black's d5 pawn.
You are regaining the pawn: your bishop will take on c4.
notes.original: Regaining the pawn.

notes.text: You win the pawn back, and your bishop joins the knight in eyeing e6.
Your queen guards the attacked bishop, ready to recapture if Black's knight takes it.
You take the knight back, and your queen keeps pressing e6 alongside your knight.
You castle where Black's advanced pawns are blocked, and your rook comes into play.
Black has stopped the typical London, but Black's kingside has been left very open.
notes.original: Black has succeeded in preventing the typical London but black's kingside has been left very open.

notes.text: According to Stockfish, this gives Black counterattacking chances.
notes.original: Gives black counterattacking chances (according to Stockfish).

notes.text: Black's pawn hits your bishop, which must retreat to h2, where it is nearly trapped.
notes.original: Now the bishop must retreat to h2, where it will be essentially trapped.

notes.text: The computer still says you are ahead, and its top moves follow a less usual London setup.
notes.original: Computer still says that white is ahead but the best moves it recommends are more of the alternative London System shown in an earlier chapter.

notes.text: Stockfish gives White only a slight edge here.
notes.original: With only a slight edge for white according to Stockfish.

notes.text: This opens your light bishop's diagonal while your knight stays clear of Black's g-pawn.
Knight to f3 is a typical London move, but it is not a good idea here.
notes.original: A typical London move but not a good idea here!

notes.text: Your pawn stops Black's h-pawn chasing your bishop and attacks the undefended g5 pawn.
Your bishop takes its best diagonal and covers e4 against Black's knight jump.
With f3 covered by Black's pawn, your knight goes through e2 toward f4.
Black's two bishops could cause you trouble if you aren't paying attention.
notes.original: The two black bishops could cause trouble if white isn't paying attention.

notes.text: Your pawn backs up d4 and lets your queen reach b3 to hit the b7 pawn.
Hitting the bishop doesn't solve the problem; Black simply retreats it.
notes.original: This doesn't solve the problem.

notes.text: This prepares to bring your other knight to f3.
notes.original: Preparing Nf3.

notes.text: Your knight blocks the bishop's pin on e2, with the other knight ready to recapture.
Your pawn hits the bishop, so it must trade on f3 or back away.
Retaking with the knight keeps your pawns tidy and keeps watch over e5.
With the pin gone, your pawn props up d4 and lets the light bishop out.
Your queen guards the b2 pawn that Black's queen was attacking.
Swapping queens suits neither side, because it opens the a-file for the opponent's rook.
notes.original: Swapping queens won't be good for either player as it will open the a-file for the opponent's rook.

notes.text: Your queen sidesteps the pawn and still guards b2, without swapping queens.
You develop and get ready to castle, happy to let Black trade on f4.
Your pawn takes back and grips e5, and the e-file half-opens for your rooks.
You are slightly better, but this won't be a typical London middlegame.
notes.original: White is slightly better but like in the other anti-Londons it will likely not be a typical London middlegame.

notes.text: Black's queen move practically forces you to castle queenside.
notes.original: Essentially forcing white to castle queenside.

notes.text: Black pushes the b-pawn to gain queenside space.
notes.original: Now

notes.text: Now Black has good chances on the queenside.
notes.original: Now black has good queenside chances.

notes.text: Your pawn chases the bishop again and grabs kingside space while it retreats.
Your pawn backs up d4 and the bishop, and opens the diagonal for your other bishop.
Black's h-pawn move frees the h7 square for the bishop in case your knight goes to h4.
notes.original: Leaving the h7 square free for the bishop in case of Nh4.

notes.text: Recapturing with the knight is fine for you.
notes.original: This is fine for white.

notes.text: If Black trades bishops here, your h-pawn recaptures and opens the file for your rook.
Taking with the h-pawn opens the file, so your rook already hits h7.
Your pawn backs up d4 and lets your bishop out toward d3.
Your knight jumps into the centre, backed by the d4 pawn, hitting d7 and f7.
You are doing well in this position.
notes.original: White is doing well here.

notes.text: Your pawn recaptures and hits the knight, driving away the defender of h7.
Your bishop lines up with the rook on h7, and your queen can join on h5.
Black left the e-pawn undefended, so your bishop simply takes it.
Your bishop steps back from the f-pawn's attack and you keep the extra pawn.
Your bishop sidesteps the pawn again and still eyes c7 along its diagonal.
Your c-pawn challenges the d5 pawn while Black has spent a move on the flank.
